implementation_notes: The JDK already provides the special cases for its own interfaces - Collections.emptyList(), emptyMap() and List.of() for collections, Optional.empty() for optional results, and OutputStream.nullOutputStream() for a sink - so returning the shipped instance is the whole implementation. The same idiom applied to a domain type is a stateless enum singleton (enum NoDiscount implements DiscountPolicy { INSTANCE; ... }), which guarantees one instance without a class hierarchy or a double-checked lock. Optional is not a replacement: it forces the caller to decide, whereas the special case lets the caller keep calling, so choose between them by asking whether absence must stay visible.
pitfalls: An empty collection and 'not loaded' are different states: returning Collections.emptyList() for a failed query turns an error into 'no results', which the JDK itself cannot distinguish.
Optional is a return type for callers who must branch; burying Optional.empty() in fields or parameters usually means a special-case type was the better answer.

Managed entities cannot simply be replaced by a hand-written implementation - persistence frameworks need their own proxies - so the decision belongs in the repository or mapper that performs the lookup.

variants.name: Sealed interface with an empty variant and exhaustive switch
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface + data-less record variant + exhaustive switch
variants.implementation_notes: From Java 21 the case can be modelled as data: a sealed interface whose permitted subtypes include a data-less record (or enum singleton) for the degenerate case, with switch pattern matching over the hierarchy so the compiler proves that every consumer handles it. This trades the pattern's silent polymorphism for visibility - the caller sees the variant - so pick it when the degenerate case must be observable but should still be a first-class value of the type, and keep the classic no-op implementation when call sites must stay branch-free.
pitfalls: All permitted subtypes must be declared in the same module or package, so a client module cannot add its own special case to the hierarchy.
An exhaustive switch is a compile-time contract: adding a variant breaks every switch, which is the point but also a source-compatibility cost for published APIs.
Pattern matching for switch needs Java 21; on older releases only preview builds accept it, so the sealed variant must not be assumed available just because records exist.
